html:
Logix Connect is a PLC training workstation that runs in a browser (and, wrapped, as a Windows app and a phone app). It puts three things on one screen that in a plant are three separate things: a controller styled on a CompactLogix with Studio 5000-style editing, a chassis of I/O modules that the controller scans, and a machine wired to that I/O: one of the graded levels, a classic scene, or the sandbox, where you lay the machine out yourself from a palette of parts.

The controller is real in the ways that matter for learning. It scans: inputs are read, the ladder is solved rung by rung, top to bottom, left to right, outputs are written, and it does that again every 20 ms. Tags are typed (BOOL, DINT, TIMER…), I/O lives at module addresses (Local:1:I.Data.0), alias tags give those addresses names, routines are called from a main routine with JSR, and a rung is written in the same neutral text Studio 5000 uses when you copy a rung. Projects export to L5X and import from it. As in Logix Designer there are two copies of the program, the project you edit and the one in the controller, and a download moves one to the other (chapter 3). What it leaves out is the parts of a real controller that teach nothing about logic: no firmware, no licence.

The machine is also real in the ways that matter. Conveyors carry parts at a speed, sensors see what is physically in front of them, a gate that fires late pushes the wrong bottle, a shredder that runs with no box under it spills glass onto the floor, a capper with an empty chute leaves bottles open, and a tank runs dry if the inlet valve is never opened. The simulator does not know what you meant; it only knows what your outputs did. That is the whole point.

The chassis

Every sandbox project has the same chassis. Slot 0 is the controller, slots 1–3 are 16-point input modules, slots 4–6 are 16-point output modules, slots 7 and 9 are 4-channel analog input modules and slot 8 is a 4-channel analog output module; slots 10–12 add two more input modules and a third analog input module. A point is written the way Studio 5000 writes it: Local:<slot>:I.Data.<bit> for an input bit, Local:<slot>:O.Data.<bit> for an output bit and Local:<slot>:I.Ch<n>Data for an analog channel.

SlotModuleNamePoints

11769-IQ16DI_116 digital inputs, Local:1:I.Data.0–15
21769-IQ16DI_216 digital inputs, Local:2:I.Data.0–15
31769-IQ16DI_316 digital inputs, Local:3:I.Data.0–15
41769-OB16DO_116 digital outputs, Local:4:O.Data.0–15
51769-OB16DO_216 digital outputs, Local:5:O.Data.0–15
61769-OB16DO_316 digital outputs, Local:6:O.Data.0–15
71769-IF4AI_14 analog inputs, Local:7:I.Ch0Data–Ch3Data
81769-OF4AO_14 analog outputs, Local:8:O.Ch0Data–Ch3Data
91769-IF4AI_24 analog inputs, Local:9:I.Ch0Data–Ch3Data
101769-IQ16DI_416 digital inputs, Local:10:I.Data.0–15
111769-IF4AI_34 analog inputs, Local:11:I.Ch0Data–Ch3Data
121769-IQ16DI_516 digital inputs, Local:12:I.Data.0–15

That is 80 digital inputs, 48 digital outputs, 12 analog inputs and 4 analog outputs. When you place a part in the sandbox, each of its signals takes the next free point of the right kind; the Scene sheet shows how many are in use. If a kind runs out, the part is placed but the signal has no address, and the status bar says so.

Four kinds of project

A graded level is a puzzle on a machine built from the sandbox parts, with bins that judge every part and a score against par. There are 22, each rated from Starter to Expert, and they are listed easiest first. A classic scene is a whole machine from everyday life — an elevator, a traffic intersection, a car wash, a material silo — with its I/O wired and named, for you to program. A sandbox is the open floor: you choose the parts, the I/O and the program; the sandboxes in the catalogue come with a machine already on the floor and, for the bottle line, the finished program as an answer key. A guided project is a sandbox with a lesson panel beside the ladder that walks you through a build one step at a time.

This book is mostly about the sandbox, because that is where you learn to build a machine and not just drive one; the levels are a good place to practise the instructions once you know them, and Part V takes them one at a time.
